correctness.rationale: Only the symmetric part contributes to \(q(z)=\langle Bz,z\rangle\). If \(q\) vanishes at a nonzero vector, the denominator vanishes on a nonzero pair; if \(q\) takes both signs, positive rescaling of two vectors makes the two quadratic values cancel. Conversely, a strictly positive or strictly negative quadratic form makes every nonzero-pair denominator one-signed. A coercive estimate \(|q(z)|\ge\beta\|z\|^2\) gives the uniform quotient bound, while strict positivity without coercivity is insufficient: on \(\ell^2\), \(B e_n=n^{-1}e_n\) gives unit vectors with denominator tending to zero. The actual primary source was checked: Theorem 2.1 and Theorem 2.3 literally assume only that \(B\) is bounded while dividing by the displayed quadratic denominator, and the Holling-IV application prints \(BY=(1-\mu(x))Y\) for merely \(\mu\in L^\infty\), so \(\mu\equiv1\) makes \(B=0\).

final_claim: For the feedback quotient used by Lamrani--El Harraki--Aziz-Alaoui--El Alaoui, boundedness of \(B\) alone does not make the denominator well defined: for a real Hilbert space, \(\langle Bz_1,z_1\rangle+\langle Bz_2,z_2\rangle\) is nonzero for every nonzero pair exactly when the quadratic form of the symmetric part \(S=(B+B^*)/2\) is strictly one-signed. A uniform feedback bound requires a coercive one-sign estimate, and the published Holling-IV specialization allows \(B=0\) under its printed hypotheses.
limitations: This audits the literal feedback formula and stated bounded-operator hypothesis; it does not assert that every stabilization result in the paper fails after adding an appropriate positivity/coercivity assumption.
